subject: TiltEdge: connection options (peering vs PrivateLink vs S2S) — decision inputs
messages:
From: Evan Shaw <evan.shaw@tiltedge.com>
To: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.com>
Cc: TiltEdge Networking <netops@tiltedge.com>, Lena Park <lena.park@tiltedge.com>
Date: 2026-12-02T09:12:00-08:00
Subject: Initial ask — connecting TiltEdge on-prem to Redwood Private

Hi Monica,

Thanks again for the intro call earlier. To recap our requirements: we run inference on two on-prem DCs (primary east-coast, DR west-coast). We need a secure, low-latency path from our inference cluster to Redwood Private for model pull & telemetry, and we want to minimize blast radius for secret exfil. Primary constraints:

- Strict control-plane isolation for customer-managed data (we cannot route all DC traffic to Redwood).
- Latency requirement: p95 request/response <= 60ms for control plane operations and model shard fetches.
- SOC2 auditors will want clear network segmentation and proof-of-access controls.
- Ops prefers a single management plane (no multiple VPN configurations to maintain).

We've attached a simple network diagram and a spreadsheet of the audit items. Can you send a short recommendation (peering vs PrivateLink vs site-to-site VPN) with pros/cons and an ops runbook we can show auditors?

Thanks,
Evan
TiltEdge — Infrastructure

Subject: Re: Initial ask — connecting TiltEdge on-prem to Redwood Private

Evan —

Thanks for the summary and the artifacts. Looping in Karthik (private deployments architect), Ben (product for Dedicated/Private), and Kimberly (security/compliance) to make sure we cover ops and auditor questions in one pass.

High-level guidance up front so you can circulate with auditors:

1) Short answer: all three options are viable, but they satisfy different risk/perf/operational tradeoffs.

2) Quick mapping to your constraints:
   - Low-latency, direct L3 connectivity: VPC peering (or equivalent cloud peering) offers the lowest hop count and predictable latency but requires mutual network ownership or a transit model.
   - Strong endpoint isolation + least-privilege access: PrivateLink (interface endpoints) exposes a narrowly scoped service endpoint in your VPC — better for limiting blast radius and satisfying auditors expecting limited egress targets.
   - Operational simplicity for isolated on-prem DCs: S2S VPN is the most flexible and easiest to provision quickly, but typically has higher variability in latency and is less ideal for heavy sustained traffic.

I asked Karthik to prepare a short comparison table and a recommended starting configuration with fallback modes.

Will follow with a short ops playbook.

Cheers,
Monica
Account Executive — Redwood Inference

From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>
To: Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.com>, Evan Shaw <evan.shaw@tiltedge.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>, Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-12-03T08:27:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Initial ask — connecting TiltEdge on-prem to Redwood Private

Evan / team —

Following is a concise architecture recommendation and the tradeoffs to discuss with network/security: 

Option A — VPC peering / direct interconnect (preferred for request latency sensitive workloads)- Summary: Layer 3 peering or cloud cross-connect between TiltEdge VPCs and Redwood Private VPCs. Persisted routes for control-plane subnets.
- Pros: Lowest latency and jitter; predictable throughput; simpler path for model shard downloads when pinned to specific subnets.
- Cons: More invasive — requires CIDR planning and routing changes in your side; potential transitive routing complexity if you have multiple DCs; auditors will ask about route propagation & who administers peering policies.
- Ops notes: Recommend establishing a dedicated peer for control-plane traffic only (use route filters/route tables to restrict which prefixes are exchanged). Use BGP session with prefix-lists to prevent accidental route leaks.

Option B — PrivateLink / interface endpoints (preferred for least-privilege and auditability)- Summary: Redwood exposes an interface endpoint (ENI) in your VPC or a managed, customer-facing service endpoint in our shared transit VPC; traffic flows to a single service FQDN and port set.
- Pros: Minimal network footprint on customer side; clear, auditable set of endpoints and ports; easier to prove to auditors that only a small set of services are reachable.
- Cons: Slightly higher latency vs peering due to service hop and NVA (depends on provider topology); not ideal for very high-volume model transfers unless you augment with a dedicated pull subnet or caching proxy.
- Ops notes: Recommend PrivateLink for control plane (API, telemetry, KMS calls) and use a separate data-channel (either peering or S2S) for large model pulls. We can support signed URLs and resumable pulls to limit bandwidth.

Option C — Site-to-site VPN (preferred for quick pilots or where cloud peering is restricted)- Summary: IPSec tunnel(s) between your edge and Redwood edge termination.
- Pros: Fast to stand up; works across clouds and on-prem without CIDR collisions; good for DR/backup connections.
- Cons: Variable latency, throughput capped by edge appliance; harder to scale and monitor at token-level per-VM.
- Ops notes: For production-grade performance, use dual tunnels + BGP and prefer hardware appliances with AES-NI or modern accelerators. Combine with Traffic Steering to avoid noisy neighbor effects.

Recommended hybrid pattern for TiltEdge (given auditors + latency need):
  - Use PrivateLink for control plane APIs and telemetry (least-privilege, easy to audit).
  - For model shard retrievals, prefer a peered data-plane between a restricted Redwood data VPC and TiltEdge inference subnets (or an S3-compatible cache on your side).
  - Keep an S2S VPN as a warm standby to simplify DR and provide an alternate path.

I'll attach a short checklist for your netops team (IP ranges, required ports, BGP hints, certificate thumbprints).

-Karthik
Principal Architect — Redwood Private

Subject: Re: Initial ask — connecting TiltEdge on-prem to Redwood Private

Thanks — this is helpful. A couple of clarifying Qs from our netops team after reviewing the checklist draft: 

1) For the data-plane peering you recommend, can we restrict peering to a single /27 or smaller range that only contains the model-serving VMs? Our concern is CIDR exhaustion and accidental route propagation into broader DC prefixes.

2) If we use PrivateLink for control plane, will Redwood provide mTLS between our service and the endpoint or do we need to present client certs from our side? Our auditors prefer mutual TLS for API calls.

3) For the S2S VPN warm standby, we have Juniper SRX appliances — any specific MTU/BFD recommendations to reduce fragmentation?

Appreciate a concise ops-oriented reply we can put into our runbook, then we can schedule the pilot.

—Lena
NetOps Manager — TiltEdge

From: Kimberly Park <kimberly_park@redwood.com>
To: Lena Park <lena.park@tiltedge.com>, Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.com>, Monica Patel <monica.patel@redwood.com>
Cc: Ben Carter <ben_carter@redwood.com>
Date: 2026-12-06T16:03:00-08:00
Subject: Re: Initial ask — connecting TiltEdge on-prem to Redwood Private

Lena — quick answers for your runbook (auditor-friendly language):

1) Peering scope and CIDR limits   - Yes. We strongly recommend a small dedicated prefix (eg. /28 or /27 depending on VM count). On our side we will only accept route advertisements for that prefix and implement prefix-lists to prevent leakage. Include explicit ACLs in your router config to block propagation to other DC ranges.

2) PrivateLink + mTLS   - Redwood supports client certificate authentication in front of PrivateLink endpoints. For control plane, we offer mTLS using customer-provided certs or a mutual TLS issued by our managed PKI (we can place a cert_signed_by_Redwood_CA or use your CA). We will record cert thumbprints in the audit artifact. All API calls are additionally signed at the application layer.

3) S2S VPN tuning for Juniper SRX   - MTU: set to 1400 on tunnel interfaces to avoid fragmentation across internet paths; enable Path MTU Discovery.
   - Use BFD for faster failure detection; configure BFD min interval 300ms/3 for control-plane quick failover (adjust if appliances under CPU pressure).
   - Prefer AES-256-GCM with SHA2 and support for PFS (secp256r1 or secp384r1).

Runbook next steps (actionable):
   - Action A (TiltEdge): Provide proposed /28 prefix and list of model-serving instances + FQDNs.
   - Action B (Redwood): Provision a PrivateLink service and share endpoint IDs + expected ports (443 + 8443 for telemetry).
   - Action C (TiltEdge): Stand up a peered data subnet in your VPC/edge and open a change window; sample BGP config template attached.

I'll draft a concise pdf runbook with exact commands and the artifact list for auditors and drop it in the shared drive. If that works, Monica can schedule the pilot kickoff next week.

Thanks,
Kimberly Park
Security & Compliance — Redwood Inference
